ann_124.text: Through this part, capital gains clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, slowly at first, then faster: from about 60% at none to about 6% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower.
Capital losses clearly lower it steadily, from about 60% at none to about 28% at 1887 US dollars.
This part reads only capital gains and capital losses.

ann_125.text: Through this part, a higher census sampling weight lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster, from about 62% at 66,572 to about 56% at 328,216 (on the training data only).
This part reads only the census sampling weight.

ann_126.text: Through this part, a higher education level clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, slowly at first, then faster: from about 80% at 7 to about 30% at 13 on the 1-16 scale.
The drop is clearly larger for people born in Germany, from about 77% to about 21%.
Being born in Germany by itself lowers it to about 48% through this part (on the training data only).

ann_127.text: Through this part, a missing occupation clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to about 86%, and handling or cleaning work to about 79%.
In the training data, 2231 people have a missing occupation and 1683 work as handlers or cleaners.

ann_128.text: Through this part, having some college as the highest education slightly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 60% to about 57%.
In the training data, 8695 people have some college as their highest education.

ann_129.text: Through this part, working outside the private sector and having preschool as the highest education each change a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less only slightly (on the training data only for preschool).
Switching this part off makes almost no difference to the predictions.

ann_130.text: Through this part, being born in Taiwan raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to about 72% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 49 people were born in Taiwan.

ann_131.text: This part acts on the 2417 machine operators and inspectors among 39073 training people, and 2121 of them have an income of $50,000 or less.

For the typical person it acts on (a 36-year-old White married man born in the United States, a high-school graduate at level 9 on the 1-16 scale, a machine operator in the private sector working 40 hours a week), it clearly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 75% to about 83%.
For the typical person overall, it clearly raises it from about 60% to about 71%.

ann_132.text: Through this part, not being a husband clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to about 42%.
Being born in India raises it to about 92% (on the training data only), and the rise is slightly larger for husbands than for people in other household roles.
Never having worked raises it to above 99% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this: only 9 people), for people born in India or elsewhere and for husbands or not.

ann_133.text: Through this part, being never married or otherwise not married clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to about 98%, and being separated to about 96%.
Compared with other household roles, being a child of the household clearly raises it to about 94% and being another relative to about 82%, while being a wife clearly lowers it to about 29%.
Being married to a member of the armed forces clearly lowers it to about 52%.

ann_134.text: Through this part, other service work clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to about 92%, farming or fishing to about 88% and administrative or clerical work to about 72%.
Working longer hours clearly lowers it steadily, from about 73% at 24 hours a week to about 47% at 55, and an executive or managerial job to about 53%.
Self-employment (not incorporated) raises it to about 77%, and federal government work lowers it to about 49% (on the training data only).

ann_135.text: Through this part, being older clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily, from about 73% at 22 years to about 41% at 58 years, and being a woman clearly raises it to about 85%.

Being Asian or Pacific Islander rather than White lowers it to about 51%, and being of a race other than White, Asian or Pacific Islander, or 'other' raises it to about 68% (on the training data only).

ann_136.text: Through this part, being born in the outlying US territories or Colombia raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to above 99%, in Vietnam to about 87% and in Thailand or China to about 84% (on the training data only).
Being born in Italy lowers it to about 45%, in England to about 48% and in the Philippines to about 54% (on the training data only).
Being born in Laos raises it to about 93% and in Honduras lowers it to about 39% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this: only 17 and 14 people).

ann_137.text: Through this part, a doctorate raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to about 72%, an academic associate degree to about 70% and a master's degree to about 67%, while 1st-4th grade lowers it to about 43% (on the training data only).
Having 10th grade as the highest education lowers it only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_138.text: Through this part, being a wife rather than a husband clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to about 16%, and household roles other than husband, wife, child or other relative lower it to about 42%.

Being never married or otherwise not married clearly raises it to about 98%, being separated to about 96%, being a child of the household to about 89% and being another relative to about 69%, while being married to a member of the armed forces lowers it to about 52%.
Never having worked raises it to above 99% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this: only 9 people), whether the person is a husband or a child of the household.
Being born in India raises it to about 92% (on the training data only), and the rise is slightly larger for husbands than for people in other household roles (about 76%).

ann_139.text: Through this part, a higher education level clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, slowly at first, then faster: from about 80% at 7 to about 30% at 13 on the 1-16 scale.

On top of that, a doctorate raises it to about 72%, an academic associate degree to about 70% and a master's degree to about 67%, while 1st-4th grade lowers it to about 43% (on the training data only).
Some college or 10th grade as the highest education lowers it only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_140.text: Through this part, other service work clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to about 92%, a missing occupation or farming or fishing to about 88%, handling or cleaning to about 82% and machine operating or inspecting to about 75%.
Working longer hours clearly lowers it steadily, from about 73% at 24 hours a week to about 47% at 55, and an executive or managerial job to about 53%.
Self-employment (not incorporated) raises it to about 77% and state government work to about 68%, while federal government work lowers it to about 48% (on the training data only).

ann_141.text: Through this part, being older clearly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily, from about 73% at 22 years to about 41% at 58 years, and being a woman clearly raises it to about 85%.

Being born in the outlying US territories or Colombia raises it to above 99%, in Vietnam to about 87% and in Thailand or China to about 84%, while being born in Italy lowers it to about 45% and in England to about 48% (on the training data only).
Being born in Laos raises it to about 93% and in Honduras lowers it to about 39% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this: only 17 and 14 people).

Being Asian or Pacific Islander rather than White lowers it to about 51%, and a higher census sampling weight lowers it slowly at first, then faster, from about 62% to about 56% (on the training data only).

ann_142.text: Across the whole model, capital gains and a higher education level clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, both slowly at first, then faster: from about 60% at no capital gains to about 6% at 6849 US dollars (flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower), and from about 80% at 7 to about 30% at 13 on the 1-16 education scale.
Capital losses clearly lower it steadily, from about 60% at none to about 28% at 1887 US dollars.

Being a wife rather than a husband clearly lowers it to about 16%, and being older and working longer hours clearly lower it steadily, from about 73% at 22 years to about 41% at 58 years and from about 73% at 24 hours a week to about 47% at 55.

Being never married, separated or otherwise not married clearly raises it to about 96% to 98%, other service work to about 92%, being a child of the household to about 89%, a missing occupation or farming or fishing to about 88%, and being a woman to about 85%.

Being born in the outlying US territories or Colombia raises it to above 99%, in India to about 92% and in Vietnam to about 87%, while 1st-4th grade as the highest education lowers it to about 43% (on the training data only).

Never having worked raises it to above 99% and being born in Laos to about 93%, while being born in Honduras lowers it to about 39% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this: only 9, 17 and 14 people).

ann_124.original: Output = logit P(income <= 50K) (train target y=1 is <=50K, base rate 0.761); positive = toward low income. Inputs z-scored; category names inferred from alphabetical codes, consistent with train frequencies. ROOT. HYPOTHESIS: a generalised additive logistic model, logit = 2.407 + capital + household + education + work + background, with no cross-group interactions (every hidden relu sees inputs from one feature group). Material nonlinearity: capital-gain hinge (dominant), education-years hinge, Husband indicator gate; everything else is linear or exactly affine on train (8774 and 4066 are always off, 2255/4651/5909/14057/2821/6000 always on). 47 inputs have no edges and are zero-effect entries. EVIDENCE (train n=39,073): acc 0.850, AUC 0.9064; best all-affine fit of the logit has AUC 0.9008 (residual sd 0.59 of logit sd 7.53), so ~0.0055 AUC is due to nonlinearity, mostly capital gain. ann_142.proposed: The whole model adds up separate household, education, work, capital and background effects: capital gains, a higher education level, capital losses, being a wife, older age and longer hours clearly lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, while not being married and being a woman clearly raise it.

summary.text: For a typical person (a 37-year-old White married man born in the United States, a high-school graduate in a professional job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week, with no capital gains or losses), the model predicts about a 60% chance of an income of $50,000 or less; capital gains clearly lower that, slowly at first, then faster, to about 6% at 6849 US dollars, a large change, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower.
A higher education level clearly lowers it, slowly at first, then faster: for a typical person from about 80% at 7 to about 30% at 13 on the 1-16 scale.
For people born in Germany it clearly lowers it even more, and steadily (from about 77% to about 21%).
Being a wife rather than a husband clearly lowers it to about 16%, while being never married rather than married clearly raises it to about 98%.
Being born in the outlying US territories (Guam, US Virgin Islands) or in Colombia raises it to above 99% (on the training data only).
A higher census sampling weight also lowers it, slowly at first, then faster, from about 62% to about 56% (on the training data only).

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

summary.text: The model treats a higher capital gains as clearly lowering the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster: for a typical person, it goes from about 60% at 0 US dollars to about 6% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.

The model treats a higher education level as clearly lowering the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster: for a typical person, it goes from about 80% at 7 on the 1-16 scale to about 30% at 13 on the 1-16 scale.
For a typical person, the model gives a clearly lower predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less if the person is a wife (about 16%) than if the person is a husband (about 60%).

A higher education level clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, and even more so if the country of birth is Germany (steadily for people whose country of birth is Germany): for a typical person, education level going from 7 on the 1-16 scale to 13 on the 1-16 scale moves the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 77% to about 21% if the country of birth is Germany, and from about 80% to about 30% if country of birth is something other than Germany.

This changes the prediction only slightly: for a typical person, going from country of birth other than India to India moves the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 60% to about 92% if the person is a husband, and from about 42% to about 76% if relationship in the household is something other than husband, other relative, own child, wife.
